analysis.one_liner: Bans major new federal rules for over a year unless an agency head grants an exemption.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a House vote; introduced in October 2011 with 10 Republican sponsors, it was referred to two committees and two subcommittees and died when the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have barred federal agencies from issuing most new major regulations — rules that raise business costs and touch the economy, environment, public health, or safety — from 30 days after passage through January 20, 2013. An agency head could exempt a rule by finding it necessary for an emergency, criminal enforcement, job creation, economic growth, reducing burdens, military or foreign affairs, or tax administration, and publishing that finding. In practice those exemptions were broad and discretionary, so each agency's own leadership would decide which rules were frozen.
analysis.who_benefits: Large regulated businesses. Any final rule costing $100 million or more — new air and water pollution limits, workplace safety standards, financial rules, consumer protections — would have been blocked unless the agency head chose to exempt it. Businesses would have gotten more than a year of freedom from new compliance costs and a reprieve from rules already in the pipeline, while rules that cut burdens on business were explicitly allowed to proceed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large regulated businesses facing major rules

how_it_helps.text: The bill stops agencies from issuing 'covered regulations' — final rules that increase business costs and are likely to have a $100 million or larger annual economic effect or materially affect the economy, jobs, the environment, public health or safety — until January 20, 2013.
Rules already in effect before September 1, 2011 were untouched, so businesses that had already absorbed compliance costs gained nothing, while rules not yet final were frozen.

Exemptions were available only for rules the agency head found necessary for an emergency, criminal law enforcement, job creation, economic growth, reducing regulatory burdens, military or foreign affairs, or tax administration — meaning rules that add protections for health, safety, or the environment had to clear a political finding to go forward, while rules that reduce burdens did not.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people, through delayed protections. The definition of a frozen rule explicitly includes rules affecting the environment, public health and safety, and consumer entitlements — the categories where new rules most often protect the public rather than burden business. A freeze delays those protections regardless of how strong their benefits are, and delayed rulemaking often means protections never return on schedule.
analysis.who_pays_short: People awaiting health, safety, and environmental rules

drawbacks.text: The freeze is indiscriminate: it blocks a rule protecting the public from a toxic exposure on the same terms as a rule burdening a small manufacturer, because the trigger is business cost, not whether the rule's benefits outweigh its costs.

Agencies would still be legally required to carry out statutes Congress already passed, so freezing the rules that implement them creates a gap between the law on the books and the rules that make it work, inviting litigation and uncertainty.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the cost side of the trade: the freeze's purpose was to spare businesses compliance expenses during a period of high unemployment, and it does so by postponing whatever public benefits those rules would have delivered, with no requirement that the postponement be made up later.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit — lower compliance costs and less regulatory uncertainty for businesses — is real but one-sided. It treats every major rule as a job-killer by definition, blocks protective and burdensome rules alike, and lets the rules that shrink regulation proceed while the ones that add protection stall. It buys business relief by putting a blanket hold on public protections, which is a poor trade for anyone not on the paying side of those compliance costs.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House committees and their subcommittees from October 2011 until the Congress ended in January 2013, and no vote was ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Representative Tim Griffin of Arkansas introduced the bill on October 13, 2011, and it was referred to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee and the House Judiciary Committee.
Nine Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The bill was referred to a Judiciary subcommittee on October 24, 2011 and to an Oversight subcommittee on November 2, 2011, and the action record shows nothing after that.
The 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 with the bill never reaching a committee vote or the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people, in the narrow sense that the freeze never took effect: agencies kept their authority to issue major rules on health, safety, the environment, and finance, and the public kept whatever protections were in the pipeline. The businesses that would have received a year-plus compliance holiday did not get it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary people; the regulatory freeze never happened

against.name: House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Darrell Issa, R)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee on regulatory affairs on November 2, 2011 and never brought it to a markup or vote.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its administrative-law subcommittee on October 24, 2011 and never acted further on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 sponsors were Republicans and no Democrat cosponsored, but no vote was ever taken, so opposition never had a chance to register on the record.

industries.industry: Large regulated businesses (manufacturers, energy producers, chemical and financial firms)
industries.note: The bill would have given them a blanket freeze on any major rule raising their costs through January 2013, including rules on pollution, workplace safety, and consumer protection. Their gain comes directly from postponing protections the public would otherwise receive.

Agencies would have lost the ability to issue major rules for the moratorium period, but their heads — not Congress or the courts — would have held the sole power to exempt rules, concentrating discretion in political appointees. Rules that reduce burdens were explicitly exempted, tilting the remaining rulemaking toward deregulation.
